title: Ivy marketplace mixed-traffic spike forensics & capacity tradeoffs
body:
Executive summary:
- This note captures a focused forensic run we did for Ivy Marketplace (customer POC) to understand tail-latency spikes and cost implications during mixed traffic bursts (user search + async recompute).
- Primary finding: short high-QPS microbursts (~90–180s, 80–140 QPS) create transient p99 blowups driven by cold KV-cache misses and model-variant fallbacks when Dedicated capacity autoscaler lags. Warmup + small prefix caches reduce p99 by ~55% in our runs.

POC goals and constraints:
- Goals: reproduce customer production spike, identify root cause of p99 regressions, quantify cost/latency tradeoffs for three configurations (hosted standard, hosted with prefix cache, dedicated reserved + burst policy).
- Constraints: customer wants <250ms p95 for search-like 1–2s generation prompts, budget target <$1.80 per 1k token-equivalents at steady-state. Sensitive to occasional spikes that impact UX.

Test matrix (what we ran):
- Models: rw-3b-quant (primary), rw-7b-fp16 (fallback candidate).
- Configs: A) Hosted-standard (autoscale default, no prefix cache), B) Hosted + prefix/kv-cache (30s TTL warmup on hot prefixes), C) Dedicated (2 reserved instances, burst pool 1 instance, canary fallback to rw-3b-quant-slim).
- Workloads: steady-state 10 QPS (1–2s prompts, avg 1.6k tokens/session), mixed background async recompute generating 4k token embeddings at 0.5 QPS, microburst windows of 60/120/180s stepping to 140 QPS.
- Measurement period: 6 hours per run, repeated 3 times to reduce variance. Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (generation end-to-end), median token latency, cold-start counts, KV-cache hit ratio, cost-per-token estimate, CPU/GPU utilization, autoscale events.

Environment notes (infra and versions):
- Cluster: hosted eu-west-1, A100-backed GPUs for dedicated runs, runtime v1.14.2, scheduler v0.9.7.
- Benchmark harness: k6-driven traffic captured with internal harness (GITHUB-PR-4587), event timestamps aligned to NTP.
- Observability hooks: Redwood Console traces + token-level cost breakdown enabled.

Key results (aggregated):
- Config A (Hosted-standard):
  - steady 10 QPS: p50 85ms, p95 210ms, p99 630ms
  - during 120s burst -> p50 170ms, p95 420ms, p99 1850ms (spike window peak)
  - cold-starts observed: 18 events per 120s-burst (workers spin up), KV-cache hit ratio: 12%
  - estimated incremental cost during burst: 2.1x baseline token cost (short window premium)

- Config B (Hosted + prefix/kv-cache):
  - steady 10 QPS: p50 80ms, p95 190ms, p99 290ms
  - during 120s burst -> p50 130ms, p95 260ms, p99 820ms
  - cold-starts observed: 6 events per 120s-burst, KV-cache hit ratio: 48% after warmup
  - notes: pre-warming hot prefixes before known sale windows reduced p99 substantially; cost overhead for caching layer ~+6% steady-state but reduced burst marginal cost by ~45%

- Config C (Dedicated reserved + burst):
  - steady 10 QPS: p50 70ms, p95 160ms, p99 240ms
  - during 120s burst -> p50 100ms, p95 210ms, p99 410ms
  - cold-starts observed: 2 events (burst instance initialization), KV-cache hit ratio: 36% (local per-node caches)
  - cost: higher fixed monthly commitment but lower per-token incremental cost during sustained bursts; for 30% time-in-burst scenario dedicated breaks even with hosted at approx 3.5M tokens/day

Interpretation and root-cause hypotheses:
- Main contributor to p99 spikes in Hosted-standard is autoscaler lag + cold KV cache. When bursts arrive, autoprovisioned workers take tens of seconds to be fully warmed and token-generation kernel paths show inefficiencies for first few requests.
- Secondary contributor: model-variant fallback policy triggers when per-worker queue depth exceeds threshold; fallback to heavier rw-7b-fp16 for certain routed requests doubled some tail latencies — routing policy needs smoothing.
- Observed that background async workloads (embeddings) compete for GPU memory bandwidth, increasing latency variability.

Mitigations tested and effectiveness:
- Prefix/KV caching (Config B): high impact on reducing p99 for search-like hot prefixes. Implementation detail: 30s TTL, async background refresh for top-500 prefixes reduced cold miss penalty. Effective for predictable traffic patterns (seasonal sales).
- Autoscale tuning: decreased scale-out cooldown from 45s to 12s lowered cold-start counts by ~60% in tests but increased churn in quiet periods. Recommend conditional cooldown tied to recent spike detection.
- Routing policy change: add a small randomized routing delay + queue-aware backpressure to avoid bulk fallback to rw-7b; reduced fallback incidents from 12% to 3% during bursts in trial.
- Dedicated baseline: best p99 stability but requires commitment; good option for customers with regular predictable bursts or strict SLOs.

Operational playbook (practical suggestions):
- Short term (customer workshop): enable prefix cache for search endpoints, set up pre-warm jobs before scheduled sale windows, reduce autoscale cooldown for heavy-read endpoints, add traffic shadowing for new routing rules.
- Medium term: introduce predictive warmup (simple heuristic based on recent rate-of-change), evaluate lightweight model distillation for fallback variant to avoid heavy fallbacks, instrument per-request memory-bandwidth metrics.
- Long term: offer a low-latency burst plan (Dedicated-lite) with warm standby nodes and billed as burst-minutes to avoid full reserved-commit.

Open questions / unknowns:
- What is the customer’s tolerance for the small additional steady-state cost for prefix caching? (customer finance TBD)
- How frequently do real-world bursts exceed 3 minutes? Our tests used 60/120/180s windows but production may have different shapes. Need historical telemetry from customer to tune.
- Are there any encrypted payload constraints that limit our ability to use shared prefix caches across customers? (security review)

Next steps and action items (who/when):
- Asha: prepare short demo showing Config B gains for next week’s customer workshop (due 2028-07-20).
- Marco: PR to runtime repo for cooldown tuning experiment (GITHUB-PR-4587) and link to canary test (due 2028-07-22).
- Leah: collect historical spike shapes from customer telemetry and upload to Confluence (CONFLUENCE-IVY-POC-2) by 2028-07-19.
- Priya & Samir: cost model write-up comparing hosted+cache vs dedicated under 3 usage profiles (low, medium bursty, high sustained) due 2028-07-25.

Appendix (raw artifacts):
- Raw CSV latency dumps attached in linked artifacts (GITHUB-PR-4587/artifacts/latency-dumps.zip).
- k6 workload scripts: scripts/ivy-mixed-burst.js in the PR.
- Quick graph pointers: Console dashboard "ivy-poc/burst-compare" (internal link in Slack thread).

Notes to self (informal):
- Remember to flag the model fallback threshold in config — current default too aggressive.
- Customer asked about on-prem option; dedicated-lite might map well to their compliance ask but need finance calc.
- This doc can seed a short one-pager for sales: "Ivy Marketplace: Burst resilience patterns".

End of note.
